title: Overlay-tree linker streams MoE experts into fixed HBM slots
idea: Revive 1960s overlay trees (IBM 7090/1401 linkers): the model compiler builds a static overlay tree with a resident root (attention, router, shared experts) and N fixed overlay slots, and experts load from LPDDR/NVMe into those slots one layer ahead using a cheap speculative router run on layer L's hidden state. Overlay loads are fixed DMA scripts generated at compile time, not demand paging.
why: Capacity: MoE models leave 90%+ of weights idle per token; holding only root plus slots cuts HBM footprint 3-6x for small-batch serving with <10% latency hit when routing prediction is >90% accurate.

title: Drum optimum-programming assembler that fills every opened DRAM row
idea: Port the IBM 650 SOAP idea (place each word where the drum will be when it is needed) to DRAM rows: a placement pass lays out embedding rows, sparse KV blocks and gather targets so bytes consumed together by one kernel share one 1-2 KB row, keeping re-transposed copies per consumer when reuse justifies it. The memory controller then replays a compile-time row schedule instead of reacting to random requests.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): raising useful bytes per activation from ~1/128 to ~1/4 cuts random-access energy 10-30x and frees channel bandwidth, so fewer DRAM devices meet the same throughput.

title: Mercury-delay-line weight carousel shared by a whole rack
idea: Like a mercury delay line, where data recirculates and any tap reads it as it passes, one copy of the model weights streams continuously from a single dense store around an optical WDM ring that passes every accelerator in a rack. Each accelerator forms its batch, multiplies the weights as they fly by and waits for the next revolution, keeping only KV cache and activations locally.
why: Capacity: replaces N per-accelerator weight copies with one per rack (8-64x less weight HBM/DRAM); a 70 GB model on a 10 Tb/s ring revolves every ~56 ms, inside decode-step budgets for throughput serving.

title: Diode-matrix ROM reborn as hybrid-bonded via-programmed weight layer
idea: Revive the 1950s diode-matrix ROM: frozen base-model weights are encoded by the presence and size of vias (2-3 bits per via resistance class) in a mature-node ROM wafer hybrid-bonded under the accelerator, with one programmable via mask per model. Bitlines feed straight up into the MAC arrays.
why: Capacity/cost: weights (50-80% of inference memory) leave HBM, which is then sized for KV only; via-ROM at ~2F^2 per 2-3 bits on a 28 nm wafer has no capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, roughly 5-10x lower cost per bit than DRAM.

title: Game-cartridge model distribution: sealed ROM weight modules sold per version
idea: Copy the NES/Game Boy cartridge business: model vendors ship each release as a sealed, keyed module of wide-parallel mask-ROM dies that plugs into a standard high-bandwidth slot on inference servers. Upgrades are cartridge swaps, the weight license rides with the hardware, and retired cartridges flow to a secondary market for edge and enterprise boxes.
why: Moves static-weight storage, 40-70% of DRAM bought for inference fleets, out of the scarce DRAM market into mask-ROM made on depreciated fabs; also keeps plaintext weights out of DRAM.

title: CDC 6600 Extended Core Storage rebuilt on fully depreciated DRAM fabs
idea: Revive ECS, the CDC 6600's huge, slower, block-transfer-only memory: build a wide (1-4 KB block), ~1 us bulk tier from 2x-nm-era DRAM lines whose tools are fully depreciated, reached only by a block-copy instruction with no load/store and no coherence. Compilers and runtimes explicitly stage tiles from ECS into a much smaller fast DDR5/HBM.
why: Fact 4 (depreciation ~55% of wafer cost): zero-depreciation old-node bits with relaxed timing approach leading-edge cost per bit without EUV; keeping only the hot 20-30% in fast DRAM roughly halves premium DRAM demand.

title: Burroughs B5000 segment descriptors carrying a per-object codec
idea: Revive B5000 descriptors and presence bits: every allocation gets a hardware descriptor with exact length, presence bit and codec ID (zero, constant, delta, dictionary, bf16-exponent entropy), and touching an absent or compressed segment traps to a decompress engine in the memory controller. Segments are stored at their compressed byte size, so there is no 4 KB/2 MB page rounding.
why: Capacity: removes page-granularity fragmentation (10-30% in KV block pools and heaps) and adds 1.5-2.5x typed compression, about 2-3x effective server DRAM.

title: Lisp-machine CDR-coding deletes adjacent pointers from managed heaps
idea: Generalize MIT/Symbolics Lisp-machine cdr-coding: the garbage collector lays objects out in traversal order and a 2-bit tag per word says 'next reference is the adjacent object', so the load unit synthesizes that address and the 8-byte pointer is never stored. Applies to Java/Go/Python heaps, graph databases and B-trees.
why: Pointers are 30-50% of bytes in managed heaps and graph stores, a large share of datacenter DRAM; eliding adjacent-object pointers recovers 15-30% of that capacity at near-zero CPU cost.

title: Ershov hash-consing of tensor blocks across fine-tunes and agent forks
idea: Revive Ershov's 1958 hash-consing in the memory controller: every 4 KB weight or KV block is content-hashed on write and interned in a global table, so identical blocks across fine-tuned variants, unmerged adapters, forked agent contexts and replicas are stored once, and near-identical blocks are stored as base pointer plus XOR-compressed residual. Divergence triggers copy-on-write.
why: Capacity: multi-tenant pools of hundreds of partial fine-tunes and agent trees are mostly duplicate blocks; 5-50x reduction for those pools.

title: Bell Labs ADPCM codec compresses KV cache along token axis
idea: Put a G.726-style adaptive differential PCM codec in the HBM base die: each key/value channel is predicted from the previous two tokens by a 2-tap adaptive predictor and only a 3-bit residual with adaptive step size is stored, decoded by a tiny MAC in the read path. Full-precision 'key frames' every 64 tokens bound drift.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory; exploiting token-to-token correlation gives 4-5x KV shrink beyond plain per-value quantization, freeing HBM for batch.

title: Telegraph codebook KV: position-free phrase blocks shared rack-wide
idea: Like 1880s commercial telegraph codes that replaced common phrases with five-letter codewords, frequently reused segments (system prompts, tool schemas, popular documents) get codewords whose KV is computed once in a position-independent form and kept in rack-pooled memory. Sessions store only codeword references, and RoPE re-rotation plus a small boundary-correction pass place the phrase at any offset at read time.
why: Unlike prefix caching, reuse works anywhere in the context; for agent/RAG workloads where 50-90% of tokens are repeated chunks, per-session KV drops 2-10x.

title: CTSS roll-out during user think time with keystroke-predicted roll-in
idea: Revive CTSS swapping between interactive turns: a chat session's KV is rolled out to CXL or flash as soon as a reply finishes, and the client streams typing telemetry (focus, keystroke cadence, draft length) so a predictor rolls the KV back into HBM in the last 1-2 s before the user hits send.
why: Users spend 20-120 s between turns versus ~5 s of generation; HBM held per concurrent session falls 5-20x without the recompute penalty of plain eviction.

title: Denning working-set billing for cloud memory
idea: Price cloud memory by each VM/container's measured working set (Denning 1968, sampled by WSClock in the hypervisor) instead of reserved GiB, auto-demoting untouched pages to compressed or far tiers and exposing the meter to developers.
why: Fleets typically touch 40-60% of allocated DRAM; a price signal on working set plus transparent demotion lets providers buy 25-40% less DRAM for the same customers.

title: Erlang-B trunk dimensioning for rack-pooled CXL memory
idea: Treat servers' memory peaks like telephone call traffic: the rack shares a CXL memory 'trunk' sized with Erlang-B for a 0.1% blocking target, and blocked requests overflow to compressed swap the way blocked calls overflowed to alternate routes. Each server keeps only its base load locally.
why: Per-server peak provisioning wastes the peak-to-mean gap; statistical multiplexing over 32-64 servers cuts rack DRAM 30-45%.

title: Holographic page memory revived as optical attention-key correlator
idea: Revive 1970s Bell/RCA holographic page memory as a correlator: a context's key vectors are written as superimposed Fourier holograms in a rewritable photorefractive crystal, and illuminating it with the query on an SLM produces every query-key dot product at once on a photodetector array. Only the top-k value rows are then fetched from DRAM.
why: Keys are half the KV cache and every key is read every token; optical key storage halves KV DRAM and cuts key-read energy 10-100x at long context.

title: STARAN associative processor as near-memory KV pre-filter
idea: Revive the Goodyear STARAN associative array: a TCAM beside the HBM stack holds a 64-bit SimHash of each cached key, the query hash is broadcast, and match lines fire for keys within a Hamming threshold. Only those ~1-3% candidates are fetched at full precision while the rest of the KV sits compressed in a slower tier.
why: Attention reads the full KV every token; a parallel associative pre-filter cuts KV bandwidth 10-50x and lets 70-90% of KV live outside HBM.

title: Differential-analyzer integrators hold sequence state instead of KV cache
idea: Revive analog computers, where state lived as voltage on integrators: state-space or linear-recurrent layers run on arrays of switched-capacitor integrators whose capacitor voltages are the recurrent state, updated per token and digitized only at layer outputs. Context length no longer grows memory.
why: For SSM/hybrid models a fixed few hundred KB of analog state per sequence replaces a KV cache that reaches tens of GB at 1M tokens, and state read/write energy disappears.

title: ICL DAP bit-plane storage with early-terminating dot products
idea: Store weights and keys as bit planes like the ICL Distributed Array Processor, MSB plane first, and compute dot products plane by plane, stopping as soon as the running bound proves an output's sign or top-k membership. Low-order planes are fetched only for close calls and live in a cheap slow tier.
why: On average 3-4 of 8 planes are needed, so 2-4x less HBM traffic, and only high planes need premium DRAM.

title: Radar MTI cancellers: store only frame-to-frame activation changes
idea: Copy radar moving-target-indicator cancellers, which stored one sweep in a delay line and subtracted the next: video and streaming-sensor models keep a reference activation map and store and propagate only entries whose change exceeds a threshold, as sparse deltas, refreshing the reference every N frames.
why: Static-camera and robot streams change <10% of activations per frame; activation memory and bandwidth drop 5-20x for video-analytics fleets.

title: No.1 ESS program-store/call-store split by page write rate
idea: The 1965 No.1 ESS kept programs in a read-mostly twistor 'program store' and live call data in a small writable ferrite 'call store'. Revive the split: the hypervisor classifies pages by measured write rate, placing read-mostly pages (weights, code, static tables) on denser memories with slow or endurance-limited writes (NOR-like, ReRAM, PCM) and only write-hot pages in DRAM.
why: Read-mostly data is 50-70% of AI server bytes; memories that fail as DRAM replacements on endurance become DRAM capacity substitutes, cutting DRAM per server 40-60%.

title: Audio-RAM revival: partially defective DRAM for error-tolerant data
idea: In the 1980s DRAMs with bad bits were sold as 'ARAM' for answering machines. Revive it: dies and HBM stacks that fail test get a stored fault map and are sold for error-tolerant data, with the allocator putting activations, gradients and low-order weight bits on faulty regions and sign/exponent bits on clean ones.
why: Supply: turns part of the 20-30% HBM/DRAM yield loss into usable cheap capacity, adding several percent to world bit supply with no new fab.

title: Bubble-memory bootloop maps let partial-capacity HBM stacks ship
idea: Magnetic bubble chips shipped with a bootloop PROM listing bad minor loops, which controllers simply skipped. Apply it to HBM/DDR: instead of scrapping stacks with dead pseudo-channels or subarrays, burn a bootloop map into the base die, sell 20/24/28 GB SKUs, and have the controller and OS remap around dead regions at subarray granularity.
why: Fact 6 (HBM yield down 20-30%): recovering most failing stacks as lower-capacity SKUs raises usable HBM bits per wafer 10-25%.

title: Briggs log-table interpolation for cross-layer KV cache
idea: Henry Briggs printed logarithms only at anchor points plus difference columns for interpolation. Store full KV only for anchor layers (every 4th) and, for in-between layers, a per-head low-rank correction to the linear interpolation of the neighbouring anchors' KV, reconstructed on the fly in the read path.
why: KV capacity 2.5-3.5x smaller with the correction term holding accuracy, and stackable with quantization.

title: Fairchild CCD serial memory revived as sequential weight streamer
idea: Revive 1975 CCD serial memories (serial-parallel-serial organization): a double-poly CCD chip built at 0.5-1 um in a university nanofab holds weights as charge packets that shift past one output amplifier per register in exactly the order inference reads them every token. Circulation regenerates charge, so there is no refresh controller, row decoder or storage capacitor.
why: Weights are read strictly sequentially, so random access is wasted; CCD needs ~2-4F^2 and no capacitor or contact per bit, a periphery-free (fact 7) weight tier that takes weights out of DRAM, demonstrated in a university fab and then moved to any image-sensor fab.

title: Bubble major/minor loops in Co/Pt tracks rotate KV each token
idea: Revive the bubble chip's major/minor-loop layout with university-sputtered Co/Pt perpendicular films whose tracks are defined by ion irradiation: each minor loop holds one KV block as magnetic domains, all loops shift together under spin-orbit-torque current, and the whole KV cache passes the readout once per decode step.
why: Attention reads all KV every token, so a nonvolatile rotating store matches the access pattern with zero standby power and no refresh, moving long-context KV out of DRAM.

title: Williams tube rebuilt with Spindt emitters over unpatterned charge target
idea: Revive the Williams/BEAMOS tube in flat form: a university-fabricated Spindt field-emitter array gated by row/column lines addresses spots on an unpatterned SiO2-on-Si charge-storage target a few microns away in vacuum. Bits are written by secondary-emission charging and read as target current, so the storage plane needs no cell lithography and no per-bit transistor.
why: A bulk capacity tier with near-zero cell processing (no EUV, no capacitor, no tungsten) behind a much smaller DRAM cache; addressing lives entirely in a reusable emitter array.

title: Plated-wire NDRO memory for read-mostly tensors
idea: Revive Apollo-era plated wire: electroplate a 1 um NiFe film with circumferential anisotropy around lithographed copper lines, cross them with word straps, and read non-destructively by sensing the small magnetization tilt a word pulse causes, writing with coincident word and bit currents. Every step is UV litho, sputtering and plating.
why: Non-destructive readout means no restore cycle and no page overfetch (fact 8); a nonvolatile, unlimited-read tier for weights and embeddings moves read-mostly data off DRAM at zero standby power.

title: Bell Labs 1952 ferroelectric matrix read by small-signal capacitance
idea: Revive Anderson's transistor-less ferroelectric crossbar in sputtered HZO or sol-gel PZT, but read it without switching: a small AC probe senses the polarization-dependent capacitance (the C-V butterfly asymmetry, enhanced by an imprint layer), so reads are non-destructive and fatigue-free, and V/3 biasing limits half-select disturb on rare writes.
why: A transistor-free 4F^2 stackable crossbar with unlimited reads and no restore holds read-mostly AI data outside DRAM, built with ALD/sputter and two metal layers.

title: IBM 360 card-capacitor ROM stacked as thin-film back-end layers
idea: Revive CCROS, the System/360 card-capacitor read-only store: each layer is a word-line metal, a thin dielectric and a bit-line metal, with a '1' wherever an e-beam-defined coupling pad exists, and pulsing a word line couples charge onto the bit lines with no transistor or diode in the array. Dozens of layers stack using only deposition and patterning.
why: A 3D frozen-weight ROM made entirely from back-end steps any university nanofab has; multi-level pad sizes give 2 bits per crossing, so weights cost a few patterning steps per layer instead of DRAM.

title: 1970s SAW radar convolver computes long convolutions without buffers
idea: Revive surface-acoustic-wave convolvers from 1970s radar: on thin-film LiNbO3 or AlN, the input sequence launches as an acoustic wave past interdigital taps weighted by the filter kernel, and the summed tap output is the convolution, so neither the sliding input window nor the kernel ever sits in memory.
why: Long-convolution/SSM layers and audio/RF front ends need large sliding buffers and kernel reads; doing them in the acoustic domain removes those DRAM/SRAM buffers and their bandwidth.

title: Transfluxor multi-aperture cells as analog non-destructive weight multipliers
idea: Revive RCA's 1955 transfluxor as electroplated planar permalloy elements with two apertures: the flux set around the small aperture is an analog weight level that gates how much of an input read pulse couples to the output winding, without disturbing the stored flux. Arrays of them perform weight-times-input in place.
why: Compute-in-memory with nonvolatile, unlimited-read magnetic weights, so weights are never fetched from DRAM; litho plus NiFe plating only.

title: Goto parametron phase memory as attractor-based retrieval store
idea: Revive the 1954 parametron, which stored bits as 0 or pi oscillation phase: a university-fab array of MEMS or LC parametric oscillators, coupled through programmable capacitors that encode stored patterns, relaxes from an injected query to the nearest stored pattern. This gives associative recall of documents or KV clusters without scanning memory.
why: Vector databases and long-term memory stores sitting in DRAM become a physical attractor network, and one settling event replaces reading GBs of embeddings.

title: Dekatron-style ferroelectric counting capacitor tracks page hotness
idea: Like dekatron tubes that stepped one state per pulse, a sub-coercive ferroelectric capacitor switches a fixed fraction of its domains on each access pulse, accumulating a nonvolatile count. One capacitor per 64 KB region sits in a small university-built HZO array beside the memory controller and is read and reset each epoch to drive tier migration.
why: Tiering saves DRAM only if hotness is known; a one-capacitor analog counter gives per-region access counts with no SRAM counter tables, enabling 30-50% smaller fast tiers.

title: Core-memory read-modify-write: accumulate inside the restore cycle
idea: Core memories rewrote every word they read, and machines like the PDP-1 used that rewrite to increment memory in place. Do the same on destructive-read arrays: a sense amplifier with an adder/XOR in its writeback path folds an incoming gradient or count into the data during restore, demonstrated on a university-fab 1T1C or gain-cell test array.
why: Gradient accumulation and embedding/histogram updates dominate training memory traffic; accumulating during restore removes double-buffered accumulators and halves read-plus-write traffic.

title: Zuse Z1 mechanical memory reborn as buckled-beam NEMS bits
idea: Revive the Z1's sliding-plate mechanical memory as university-etched buckled Si or SiN nanobeams with two stable positions: reads sense capacitance to a fixed electrode without moving the beam, and electrostatic pulses snap it over on rare writes.
why: Zero leakage, no refresh (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power) and unlimited reads make a store for weights and static tables that sits outside DRAM.

title: Widrow memistor: electroplated analog weights trained in place
idea: Revive Widrow's 1960 memistor, a resistor whose conductance was set by electroplating copper: micro-fabricated three-terminal cells with a solid electrolyte set conductance by gate current, so one analog crossbar both stores and updates weights during training.
why: Training keeps weights, gradients and Adam states (~16 bytes/param) in DRAM; in-place analog update removes most of that, a 5-10x memory cut for on-device learning.

title: Goto-pair tunnel-diode CAM as hardware hash-cons index
idea: Revive the 1960s Goto pair, two series tunnel diodes that latch a bit with no transistor, as the storage element of a CAM cell: Esaki diodes made by degenerate spin-on doping in a university fab form a dense CAM that holds content hashes and answers 'is this block already stored?' in one cycle for inline memory dedup.
why: Inline dedup needs a huge, fast hash index that today eats DRAM; a native associative store makes dedup feasible at memory speed, 1.3-3x effective capacity on duplicate-heavy servers.

title: Core-plane-sized memory sheets on display glass as cold tier
idea: Core planes were big, cheap, hand-woven panels; revive the form factor as large-area memory on glass: 2 um-rule oxide-TFT gain cells patterned on glass sheets (prototyped on 4-6 inch glass in a university nanofab) and read through edge-mounted silicon sense chips, giving ~30 GB per square metre at ~1 us.
why: Glass processing costs ~100x less per area than silicon; a microsecond cold tier shrinks DRAM to the hot set and draws on display fabs instead of DRAM fabs.

title: Strowger bank switching with university MEMS relays for memory pooling
idea: Revive 8-bit bank switching and Strowger stepping switches: an array of university-fabricated ohmic MEMS relays physically re-points DDR channels between hosts, so a memory module moves to another server in microseconds with no copy, no CXL controller and no protocol latency once connected.
why: Racks provision memory for average rather than peak demand through passive re-pointing, ~30% less DRAM, without the cost and latency of CXL switches.

title: Setun balanced-ternary cells for native 1.58-bit weights
idea: Revive the 1958 Setun computer's balanced-ternary storage: a university-built crossbar in which each cell holds -1/0/+1 as two complementary ferroelectric states, and the bitline sums currents with sign, so ternary MACs need no multiplier and each weight costs log2(3) bits.
why: Ternary (BitNet-style) models need ~10x less weight memory than fp16; native ternary cells avoid 2-bit padding (26% overhead) and keep weights out of DRAM entirely.

title: Goodman shadow-casting optical multiplier with laser-written weight masks
idea: Revive Goodman's 1978 incoherent optical matrix-vector multiplier: an LED/microLED row carries the input vector, light passes through a grayscale weight mask written by the university laser writer or e-beam, and a photodiode column sums each row; swapping masks swaps models.
why: Weights become a photomask instead of DRAM bits and are read by photons in parallel, so fixed edge models need no weight memory or weight bandwidth.

title: Williams-tube leaky charge stores optimizer momentum without refresh
idea: Williams tubes lost charge and needed regeneration; here decay is the feature: momentum/Adam moment buffers live as analog charge on a university-built capacitor array whose leakage time constant is tuned to the beta decay per step, so physics performs the exponential moving average with no refresh and no digital storage.
why: Optimizer states are ~8 of 16 bytes per parameter in mixed-precision training; replacing them with leaky analog cells roughly halves training memory.

title: Core-plane inhibit wire: bit-level write suppression for low-endurance tiers
idea: Core planes used an inhibit line to stop a bit from flipping; build the same into a university-fabbed ReRAM/PCM array, where each bit driver compares new and stored data and inhibits unchanged bits so a write pulses only the bits that change.
why: Typical writes flip 10-15% of bits; 5-10x fewer device writes stretch endurance-limited memories into a write-active DRAM-substitute role, shrinking DRAM.

title: Gaines stochastic computing: noise-driven rounding removes FP32 master weights
idea: Revive Gaines' 1967 stochastic computing by putting true-random noise sources (university-fabbed avalanche diodes or RTN transistors) in the memory write path, so every weight update into a bf16/fp8 store is stochastically rounded in hardware at no compute cost.
why: Unbiased stochastic rounding lets training drop FP32 master weights and FP32 optimizer copies, ~2-4x less training memory.

title: SAGE-model university memory production for strategic buyers
idea: Core memory for SAGE was first built at MIT Lincoln Lab before industry took over; repeat that: federal funding lets university nanofabs build first-run specialty memory tiers (CCD weight streamers, back-end ROM, NDRO magnetics) for defense and national-lab systems under guaranteed purchase, then transfer the proven processes to U.S. mature-node fabs.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: domestic, no-EUV memory tiers that offset DRAM demand in strategic systems and de-risk new tiers before $1B+ fab commitments.

title: Direct-view storage tube revived as bistable pixels without framebuffers
idea: Tektronix direct-view storage tubes held the image on the screen with no frame memory; revive it with university-fabricated bistable pixels (ferroelectric or cholesteric liquid crystal on a glass TFT backplane) that latch their state, so phones, laptops and thin clients send only changed regions and keep no scanout framebuffer or panel self-refresh RAM.
why: Removes 50-150 MB of scanout buffers per device plus display-refresh DRAM traffic; small per device, but LPDDR is about a third of world DRAM bits, so a 1-2% cut across billions of devices frees real supply.
